# Boiling drinking water and protecting wells (`boiled_water`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/medicine.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Medicine & hygiene (`medicine`)
- Deps: helped by contagion_theory, cholera_waterborne, water_filtration_chlorination
- Core idea: Water that looks, smells and tastes clean can carry cholera, typhoid and dysentery if excrement has reached it. Bringing it to a full rolling boil for a minute (three minutes high in the mountains) makes it safe; let cloudy water settle or strain it through cloth first. Keep boiled water in a covered, narrow-necked vessel and pour it out; never dip cups or hands in. Protect the source as well: line the well, give it a raised rim, a cover and its own clean bucket, drain spilt water away, and keep latrines, dung heaps and graves about 30 m away and downhill. Take river water upstream of the town.
- Pitfalls:
  - Trusting clear, cool or running water; 'a stream cleans itself after a few yards' is false
  - Boiling and then dirtying the water again with a dipped cup, dirty hands or an open jar
  - Believing boiling removes poisons; lead, arsenic and salt stay and become more concentrated
  - Thinking the alcohol in weak beer or watered wine makes it safe; beer is safe because the wort was boiled, and the story that medieval people drank only beer because water was deadly is a myth
  - Only warming the water instead of bringing it to the boil
- History: greece: c. 400 BC – Hippocratic Airs, Waters, Places judges health by the water and advises boiling and straining some waters; rome: 1st c. AD – Pliny records boiled drinking water (Nero's decocta); aqueducts bring spring water from outside the city; india: early centuries AD – Sushruta Samhita discusses boiling water and clarifying turbid water, including with cloth (dating disputed); china: from c. 8th c. (Tang) – tea drinking makes boiled water habitual; the health benefit is plausible but was never measured; europe: 1854 – Snow traces cholera to the Broad Street pump; 1880s Koch's bacteriology explains why boiling works
- Read:
  - Steven Johnson, The Ghost Map (2006)
  - M. N. Baker, The Quest for Pure Water (1948)
  - World Health Organization, Guidelines for Drinking-water Quality (4th ed., 2011)
